front: Why should a calling service's HTTP client timeout generally be shorter than the callee's own request-processing timeout?
back: If the caller times out and moves on (or retries) while the callee is still working, the caller stops waiting for a response it will never use, while a longer caller timeout would tie up the caller's own resources waiting past the point where it could have already given up.
accepted_answers: If the caller times out and moves on (or retries) while the callee is still working, the caller stops waiting for a response it will never use, while a longer caller timeout would tie up the caller's own resources waiting past the point where it could have already given up.
hint: The caller should never wait longer than it's willing to actually use the answer.

front: In a chain of service A calling B calling C, what problem occurs if each service independently uses the same fixed timeout (for example, 5 seconds) without a shared deadline budget?
back: Retries or delays at C can consume most of B's timeout budget before B even finishes calling C, leaving B little or no time to respond to A within A's own timeout, so failures can cascade upward even though each individual timeout looked reasonable in isolation.
accepted_answers: Retries or delays at C can consume most of B's timeout budget before B even finishes calling C, leaving B little or no time to respond to A within A's own timeout, so failures can cascade upward even though each individual timeout looked reasonable in isolation.
hint: Timeouts need to be part of a shared budget across the whole call chain, not set independently per hop.

front: What is exponential backoff in a retry strategy?
back: Each successive retry waits progressively longer (for example, doubling the delay each time) before trying again, rather than retrying immediately or at a fixed interval, giving a struggling dependency more room to recover.
accepted_answers: Each successive retry waits progressively longer (for example, doubling the delay each time) before trying again, rather than retrying immediately or at a fixed interval, giving a struggling dependency more room to recover.
hint: Each retry waits longer than the last.

front: Why is adding random jitter to exponential backoff important when many clients are retrying the same failed dependency simultaneously?
back: Without jitter, many clients that failed at roughly the same time will all retry at roughly the same future instant, recreating the same overload spike that caused the original failure; randomizing the delay spreads retries out over time instead.
accepted_answers: Without jitter, many clients that failed at roughly the same time will all retry at roughly the same future instant, recreating the same overload spike that caused the original failure; randomizing the delay spreads retries out over time instead.
hint: Synchronized backoff just recreates the thundering herd on a delay.

front: What is "retry amplification" across a multi-hop call chain, and why is it dangerous?
back: If every layer in a call chain independently retries a failure a few times, the total number of underlying attempts multiplies across layers (for example, 3 retries at each of 3 layers can become up to 27 actual attempts), which can turn a struggling downstream service's overload into a much larger overload.
accepted_answers: If every layer in a call chain independently retries a failure a few times, the total number of underlying attempts multiplies across layers (for example, 3 retries at each of 3 layers can become up to 27 actual attempts), which can turn a struggling downstream service's overload into a much larger overload.
hint: Retries at every layer compound multiplicatively, not just additively.

front: Describe the three states of a circuit breaker and when each is active.
back: Closed: requests flow normally and failures are counted; Open: after too many failures, requests fail immediately without calling the dependency, giving it time to recover; Half-Open: after a cooldown, a limited number of trial requests are allowed through to test if the dependency has recovered before fully closing again.
accepted_answers: Closed: requests flow normally and failures are counted; Open: after too many failures, requests fail immediately without calling the dependency, giving it time to recover; Half-Open: after a cooldown, a limited number of trial requests are allowed through to test if the dependency has recovered before fully closing again.
hint: Normal, then tripped-and-blocking, then cautiously testing recovery.

front: Why does a circuit breaker's "open" state actually help the failing downstream dependency recover, rather than just protecting the caller?
back: While open, the caller stops sending requests to the struggling dependency entirely, removing load from it during the exact period it needs to recover, instead of continuing to pile on requests (and their retries) that make the outage worse.
accepted_answers: While open, the caller stops sending requests to the struggling dependency entirely, removing load from it during the exact period it needs to recover, instead of continuing to pile on requests (and their retries) that make the outage worse.
hint: Stopping traffic is a mercy to the failing dependency, not just self-protection.

front: What is the bulkhead pattern, named after ship compartments?
back: Isolate resources (thread pools, connection pools) per dependency so that one slow or failing dependency can only exhaust its own allotted resources, instead of consuming shared resources that starve calls to unrelated, healthy dependencies.
accepted_answers: Isolate resources (thread pools, connection pools) per dependency so that one slow or failing dependency can only exhaust its own allotted resources, instead of consuming shared resources that starve calls to unrelated, healthy dependencies.
hint: Contain the flooding to one compartment instead of sinking the whole ship.

front: A service uses one shared thread pool for calls to both a fast internal service and a slow, occasionally-hanging third-party API. What cascading failure can result when the third-party API becomes slow?
back: Threads pile up waiting on the slow third-party calls until the shared pool is exhausted, leaving no threads available to handle requests to the fast internal service either, so an unrelated dependency's slowness takes down the entire service.
accepted_answers: Threads pile up waiting on the slow third-party calls until the shared pool is exhausted, leaving no threads available to handle requests to the fast internal service either, so an unrelated dependency's slowness takes down the entire service.
hint: A shared, unbounded resource pool lets one dependency's failure become everyone's failure.

front: What is backpressure, in the context of an overloaded service?
back: A mechanism for a service (or queue) under load to signal or enforce that producers slow down or that excess requests are rejected/queued, rather than silently accepting unlimited work it cannot actually keep up with.
accepted_answers: A mechanism for a service (or queue) under load to signal or enforce that producers slow down or that excess requests are rejected/queued, rather than silently accepting unlimited work it cannot actually keep up with.
hint: It's the system pushing back on more work instead of silently drowning.

front: What is "load shedding," and why might deliberately rejecting some requests during an overload actually improve overall availability?
back: Load shedding intentionally rejects a portion of incoming requests (often the least important, like low-priority background work) once a service is near capacity, which keeps the remaining accepted requests fast and successful rather than letting the whole service slow down or fail for every request under overload.
accepted_answers: Load shedding intentionally rejects a portion of incoming requests (often the least important, like low-priority background work) once a service is near capacity, which keeps the remaining accepted requests fast and successful rather than letting the whole service slow down or fail for every request under overload.
hint: Deliberately failing some requests can protect the majority from failing too.

front: What is a graceful degradation (fallback) response, such as showing cached or default recommendations when the recommendation service is down?
back: Returning a reduced but still useful response when a non-critical dependency fails, so the overall user experience stays functional (if less personalized or complete) instead of failing the entire request just because one optional dependency is unavailable.
accepted_answers: Returning a reduced but still useful response when a non-critical dependency fails, so the overall user experience stays functional (if less personalized or complete) instead of failing the entire request just because one optional dependency is unavailable.
hint: Degrade the experience for one broken piece instead of failing the whole request.

front: What is the difference between a Kubernetes liveness probe and a readiness probe?
back: A liveness probe checks whether the process is still functioning and should be restarted if it fails repeatedly; a readiness probe checks whether the instance is currently able to serve traffic well, and a failing readiness probe just removes it from the load balancer's rotation without restarting it.
accepted_answers: A liveness probe checks whether the process is still functioning and should be restarted if it fails repeatedly; a readiness probe checks whether the instance is currently able to serve traffic well, and a failing readiness probe just removes it from the load balancer's rotation without restarting it.
hint: One decides "should this process be killed"; the other decides "should this instance get traffic right now."

front: An instance is temporarily overwhelmed and slow, but not actually broken, and its readiness probe correctly starts failing. Why would restarting the process (as a liveness failure would) be the wrong response here?
back: Restarting a merely overloaded (but otherwise healthy) instance doesn't fix the underlying overload and just adds the cost and disruption of a restart; removing it from traffic rotation via the readiness probe until it recovers is the more appropriate response.
accepted_answers: Restarting a merely overloaded (but otherwise healthy) instance doesn't fix the underlying overload and just adds the cost and disruption of a restart; removing it from traffic rotation via the readiness probe until it recovers is the more appropriate response.
hint: Overloaded is not the same failure mode as broken; the response should match the actual problem.

front: In what order should timeouts, retries, and a circuit breaker typically be composed around an outbound call?
back: A timeout bounds each individual attempt, retries (with backoff) wrap around a bounded number of timed-out attempts, and the circuit breaker wraps the whole retrying call so that once failures cross a threshold, further calls (and their retries) are skipped entirely until the breaker allows trial requests again.
accepted_answers: A timeout bounds each individual attempt, retries (with backoff) wrap around a bounded number of timed-out attempts, and the circuit breaker wraps the whole retrying call so that once failures cross a threshold, further calls (and their retries) are skipped entirely until the breaker allows trial requests again.
hint: Bound one attempt, then bound how many attempts, then bound whether to attempt at all.

front: During a database primary failover, why might writes fail or time out for a short window even though a healthy replica exists and gets promoted?
back: Detecting the primary's failure, electing/promoting a replica to the new primary, and updating routing/DNS so clients connect to the new primary all take some non-zero time, during which no node is accepting writes as the confirmed primary.
accepted_answers: Detecting the primary's failure, electing/promoting a replica to the new primary, and updating routing/DNS so clients connect to the new primary all take some non-zero time, during which no node is accepting writes as the confirmed primary.
hint: Detection, promotion, and re-routing all take real time before writes can resume.

front: What is "split-brain" in a database failover scenario, and why is it dangerous?
back: Two nodes each believe they are the primary (for example, due to a network partition isolating the old primary rather than actually crashing it) and both accept writes independently, which can cause conflicting, divergent data that is difficult or impossible to reconcile afterward.
accepted_answers: Two nodes each believe they are the primary (for example, due to a network partition isolating the old primary rather than actually crashing it) and both accept writes independently, which can cause conflicting, divergent data that is difficult or impossible to reconcile afterward.
hint: Two "primaries" accepting writes at once means the data can permanently diverge.

front: Right after a failover promotes a replica to primary, why might a client that reads from a (different) read replica still see stale data for a while?
back: Read replicas replicate asynchronously and can lag behind the primary; the promotion changes which node is primary, but it doesn't instantly catch up every other replica's replication lag, so reads from a lagging replica can still return data older than what was just written to the new primary.
accepted_answers: Read replicas replicate asynchronously and can lag behind the primary; the promotion changes which node is primary, but it doesn't instantly catch up every other replica's replication lag, so reads from a lagging replica can still return data older than what was just written to the new primary.
hint: Promotion fixes who accepts writes; it doesn't fix existing replication lag elsewhere.

front: A request fans out to five downstream services in parallel to build one response, and two of the five calls fail while three succeed. Name two reasonable strategies for handling this partial failure.
back: Return a partial response with the successful data and clearly flag which sections are missing/degraded, or fail the entire request if all five results are required for correctness; the right choice depends on whether the missing data is essential or merely supplementary.
accepted_answers: Return a partial response with the successful data and clearly flag which sections are missing/degraded, or fail the entire request if all five results are required for correctness; the right choice depends on whether the missing data is essential or merely supplementary.
hint: Decide upfront whether each fan-out call is required or optional for a correct response.

front: Why must a retried request after a timeout be idempotent, given that the original request may have actually succeeded on the server even though the client never saw the response?
back: If the original request already completed its side effects and the client retries because it merely didn't receive the response, a non-idempotent retry (like "create order" again) would duplicate that side effect; only an idempotent retry is safe regardless of whether the first attempt secretly succeeded.
accepted_answers: If the original request already completed its side effects and the client retries because it merely didn't receive the response, a non-idempotent retry (like "create order" again) would duplicate that side effect; only an idempotent retry is safe regardless of whether the first attempt secretly succeeded.
hint: A timeout tells you the response was lost, not whether the work was actually done.

front: What is chaos engineering?
back: Deliberately injecting controlled failures (killing instances, adding latency, dropping network traffic) into a system, often in production, to verify that its resilience mechanisms (retries, failover, circuit breakers) actually work as designed rather than assuming they do.
accepted_answers: Deliberately injecting controlled failures (killing instances, adding latency, dropping network traffic) into a system, often in production, to verify that its resilience mechanisms (retries, failover, circuit breakers) actually work as designed rather than assuming they do.
hint: Test your resilience assumptions by actually breaking things on purpose.

front: Why does an unbounded, ever-growing database connection pool not actually fix an application that's slow because the database itself is overloaded?
back: The database has a finite capacity to process concurrent work regardless of how many connections are opened to it; adding more connections just means more concurrent queries competing for the same limited database resources, which can make contention (and overall latency) worse instead of better.
accepted_answers: The database has a finite capacity to process concurrent work regardless of how many connections are opened to it; adding more connections just means more concurrent queries competing for the same limited database resources, which can make contention (and overall latency) worse instead of better.
hint: More connections doesn't create more real database capacity underneath them.

front: A connection pool is sized far smaller than the number of concurrent requests trying to use it during a traffic spike. What does each request experience while waiting for a pooled connection to free up?
back: Requests queue and wait for an available connection, adding directly to their response latency; if the wait exceeds the pool's connection-acquisition timeout, the request fails with a pool-exhausted/timeout error instead of an actual database error.
accepted_answers: Requests queue and wait for an available connection, adding directly to their response latency; if the wait exceeds the pool's connection-acquisition timeout, the request fails with a pool-exhausted/timeout error instead of an actual database error.
hint: A busy pool adds queueing delay, and eventually a distinct kind of timeout, before the database is even reached.

front: Why should rate limiting be applied at a service's edge/gateway in addition to (not instead of) resilience patterns like circuit breakers deeper in the call chain?
back: Rate limiting at the edge prevents excessive load from reaching the service at all, protecting shared downstream resources proactively, while circuit breakers deeper in the chain react to failures that have already started happening; the two are complementary, not redundant.
accepted_answers: Rate limiting at the edge prevents excessive load from reaching the service at all, protecting shared downstream resources proactively, while circuit breakers deeper in the chain react to failures that have already started happening; the two are complementary, not redundant.
hint: One prevents overload from starting; the other reacts once something is already failing.

front: What does "deadline propagation" mean when service A calls service B which calls service C?
back: A's original deadline (how much total time is left before the caller gives up) is passed along to B and then to C, so every downstream hop knows how much time actually remains for the whole chain instead of each hop independently assuming it has its own full timeout budget.
accepted_answers: A's original deadline (how much total time is left before the caller gives up) is passed along to B and then to C, so every downstream hop knows how much time actually remains for the whole chain instead of each hop independently assuming it has its own full timeout budget.
hint: Pass along "how much time is actually left," not a fresh full timeout at every hop.

front: A security-critical authorization check depends on a call to an external policy service that is temporarily unreachable. Should the request typically "fail open" (allow it) or "fail closed" (deny it), and why?
back: Fail closed (deny), because for security-sensitive checks the safer default under uncertainty is to deny access rather than risk granting access that should have been denied; failing open trades a known safety property for availability in exactly the case where that trade is usually unacceptable.
accepted_answers: Fail closed (deny), because for security-sensitive checks the safer default under uncertainty is to deny access rather than risk granting access that should have been denied; failing open trades a known safety property for availability in exactly the case where that trade is usually unacceptable.
hint: When you can't verify a security decision, the safe default is to deny, not to allow.

front: Why is "fail open" sometimes the accepted choice for a non-critical dependency, such as an optional feature-flag service being unreachable?
back: If the worst case of guessing wrong is a minor, low-risk inconvenience (like showing a default feature configuration) rather than a security or correctness violation, allowing the request to proceed with a safe default often preserves availability without meaningful downside.
accepted_answers: If the worst case of guessing wrong is a minor, low-risk inconvenience (like showing a default feature configuration) rather than a security or correctness violation, allowing the request to proceed with a safe default often preserves availability without meaningful downside.
hint: The right default depends on how bad the worst case of "wrongly allowed" actually is.
